• Energy classification  
  – A letter grade (A–G) that sums up the building’s overall energy performance. If more than one declaration exists, the most recent rating is the one to rely on.  

• Measured or calculated energy use  
  – Annual delivered energy (kWh/m² year) for heating, cooling, hot water and, in some cases, appliances.  

• Key building data  
  – Building type (e.g. detached house, apartment block)  
  – Heated floor area (Atemp in m²)  
  – Number of above-ground storeys  
  – Number of stairwells  
  – Owner-builder flag (whether it was self-constructed)  

• Technical descriptions  
  – Main envelope components (walls, windows, roofs) and their U-values  
  – Heating system type, ventilation arrangement, domestic hot water system

Direct-acting electric radiators (sometimes called direct-acting convection or panel heaters) convert virtually 100 percent of the electricity they draw into heat at the point of use. In that very narrow sense they are “efficient” – no energy is lost inside the unit. However, when you consider the full energy chain (electricity generation, transmission and distribution losses), their overall efficiency and carbon footprint can be quite poor compared with other heating systems.

Key points to consider:

1. Point-of-use efficiency  
   • Since they simply pass electric current through a resistive element, virtually all of that energy becomes heat in the room.  
   • They respond very quickly to a thermostat signal – you get heat as soon as they switch on.

2. Primary energy and carbon impact  
   • If your electricity comes from fossil-fuel power stations, only around 30–40 percent of the fuel’s energy makes it to the grid. Transmission and distribution add another 5–10 percent loss.

Here are several practical tips to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators while keeping energy use and costs under control:

1. Use programmable or smart thermostats  
   • Fit each radiator with its own room thermostat or electronic temperature control.  
   • Program lower temperatures during the night or when rooms are unoccupied.  
   • Take advantage of “set-back” periods—dropping the temperature by 2–3 °C for a few hours can cut energy use significantly.

2. Zone your heating  
   • Divide your home into heating zones (e.g. bedrooms vs. living areas) so you only heat the rooms you’re actually using.  
   • In seldom-used rooms (guest rooms, storage areas), maintain a frost-protection setting (around 6–10 °C) rather than full comfort heating.

   • Keep radiator fronts and convector fins clean and dust-free to ensure proper air flow.

Natural (or “passive”) ventilation relies on wind forces and the stack effect (warm air rising) rather than electrically driven fans.  Compared to mechanical ventilation, its main advantages are:

1. Energy savings and lower operating costs  
   • No or minimal fan‐power required means significantly reduced electricity consumption.  
   • Eliminates the energy losses associated with ductwork and fan operation.

2. Reduced environmental impact  
   • Lower electricity use translates directly into reduced greenhouse-gas emissions.  
   • Fewer mechanical components mean less material and energy embodied in manufacture and maintenance.

3. Lower installation and maintenance requirements  
   • Simplified system: typically just operable windows, vents or passive inlets/outlets.  
   • No complex fans, filters or heat‐recovery units to service or replace, which reduces lifecycle costs.

4. Improved acoustic comfort  
   • Absence of fan noise and ductborne sound means quieter indoor environ

Optimizing natural ventilation in a dwelling involves careful attention to building design, orientation, component sizing and user behavior. Below are key strategies and considerations:

1. Orient and plan for cross-ventilation  
   • Place primary living spaces and bedrooms so that windows or vents face prevailing wind directions.  
   • Provide openings on at least two façades—ideally orthogonal—to induce air flow straight through the space.  
   • Use operable windows, louvers or shutters that occupants can adjust to modulate flow and draft.

In electric‐vehicle charging terminology the line between “normal” (or “slow”) charging and “fast” charging is generally drawn by the maximum power output of the charger—and whether it is AC or DC.  While exact definitions can vary by country and organization, the following thresholds are commonly used in Europe:

1. AC Charging (on alternating current)  
   • “Normal” or “slow” AC charging: up to 3.7 kW (single‐phase)  
   • “Fast” AC charging: from about 7.4 kW up to 22 kW (three‐phase)  
   • In practice, most home wallboxes are 3.7–7.4 kW, and public AC chargers often go up to 11–22 kW.  

2. DC Charging (on direct current)  
   • “Fast” DC charging: typically from 24 kW up to about 50 kW  
   • “Rapid” or “ultra‐fast” DC charging: 50 kW and above, with many modern chargers now offering 150 kW, 350 kW or more

Load balancing for electric-vehicle (EV) charging is a strategy and set of technologies that dynamically distribute available electrical power among one or more charging points so that:

• The total load on the building’s electrical installation or on the local grid never exceeds its rated capacity.  
• Each vehicle receives the maximum possible charging current without tripping breakers or forcing costly grid upgrades.  
• Peak power demand—and thus demand charges or network constraints—are minimized.

Key aspects of EV-charging load balancing:

   – Dynamic balancing continuously measures total building or feeder load (often in real time) and adjusts each charger’s output to ensure the combined draw stays within safe limits.

Recommended lighting levels in stairwells depend on the intended use of the building (residential, office, public) and whether you are referring to normal (operational) lighting or emergency/escape‐route lighting. Below are the most commonly cited targets:

1. Normal (operational) lighting  
   • Horizontal illuminance at floor/step level:  
     – Residential stairwells: 100 lux (minimum), 150 lux (recommended)  
     – Offices or public buildings: 150 – 200 lux  
   • Uniformity (minimum/average): U₀ ≥ 0.4–0.6  
   • Glare rating: Restrict to UGR < 25 in public interiors  

   These figures are drawn from the European standard SS-EN 12464-1 “Light and lighting – Lighting of work places,” which is commonly adopted in Sweden and across Europe.

2. Emergency and escape‐route lighting  
   • Per SS-EN 1838 (“Application of lighting for emergency situations”):  
     – Horizontal illuminance: at least 1 lux along the centre line of the escape route  
     – Recommended: 5–10 lux at landin

In Sweden there is no strict upper‐limit for stairwell temperature, but the Building Regulations (BBR) stipulate that unheated common areas must not fall below +12 °C in winter. In practice, for condensation control and occupant comfort most property managers aim for:

 • Minimum temperature (BBR requirement): +12 °C  
 • Recommended operational temperature: around +15 °C  
 • EPC (energideklaration) calculation assumption: +17 °C  

Keeping stairwells in the 15–17 °C range balances energy efficiency with frost protection and user comfort.
